{{Short description|Japanese term for a state of defilement}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}}
{{Italic title}}
{{nihongo3|uncleanness, defilement|穢れ・汚れ|'''Kegare'''}} is the Japanese term for a state of pollution and defilement, important particularly in {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|lt=Shinto|lt_ja=神道}} as a religious term. It is an impure state felt to be abhorrent, arising from {{ill|Death|ja|死|lt=death|lt_ja=死}}, {{ill|Epidemic|ja|疫病|lt=epidemic disease|lt_ja=疫病}}, {{ill|Sexual intercourse|ja|性交|lt=sexual intercourse|lt_ja=性交}} and the like, and believed to bring disorder to the community, which is why it is avoided.<ref>''Daijirin'', Sanseidō, "Kegare".</ref> Typical causes of ''kegare'' are contact with any form of death, childbirth (for both parents), disease and menstruation, and acts such as rape.<ref name="EOS">{{cite encyclopedia|last=Nishioka|first=Kazuhiko|title=Kegare|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1212|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref> In Shinto, ''kegare'' is a form of ''{{ill|Tsumi|ja|罪|lt=tsumi|lt_ja=罪}}'' (taboo violation), which must somehow be remedied by the person responsible, through purification rites such as ''{{ill|Misogi|ja|禊|lt=misogi|lt_ja=禊}}'' and ''{{ill|Harae|ja|祓|lt=harae|lt_ja=祓}}''.<ref>Iwanami ''{{ill|Kōjien|ja|広辞苑|lt=Kōjien|lt_ja=広辞苑}}'' Japanese dictionary, 6th edition (2008), DVD version, "Kegare".</ref><ref>Iwanami ''Kōjien'', 6th edition (2008), DVD version, "Tsumi".</ref> ''Kegare'' can harm not only the person directly affected but also the community they belong to.

''Kegare'' is not a moral judgment but a reaction to amoral natural forces; whether the defilement came from a deliberate act, such as a crime, or from an external event, such as illness or death, is secondary.<ref name="scheid"/> It is therefore not an equivalent of sin.

== The general idea of defilement ==
Washing the hands and body with water is thought to remove visible dirt and at the same time to "purify ''kegare''". Modern natural science explains washing as rinsing away pathogens, but the idea of ''kegare'' belongs to a different system of words and ideas.

The idea of defilement survives today in many religious rites, among them ''misogi'', {{ill|Abhiseka|ja|灌頂|lt=abhiṣeka|lt_ja=灌頂}} and {{ill|Baptism|ja|洗礼|lt=baptism|lt_ja=洗礼}}.

Typical things held to be defiled are death, {{ill|Disease|ja|病気|lt=illness|lt_ja=病気}}, {{ill|Childbirth|ja|出産|lt=childbirth|lt_ja=出産}}, sexual intercourse, {{ill|Woman|ja|女性|lt=women|lt_ja=女性}}, {{ill|Injury|ja|怪我|lt=injury|lt_ja=怪我}} and {{ill|Excretion|ja|排泄|lt=excretion|lt_ja=排泄}}, and things connected with them.

People from outside one's own community (people of other prefectures, foreigners, other ethnic groups) and their culture, people of particular descent or status (such as untouchables), particular occupations (entertainers, moneylenders, butchers and so on) and parts of the body (such as the left hand, which must not be used for eating) may also be treated as defiled. These are not always absolute defilements and often depend on the act: an animal may be touched, for example, but not eaten.

The idea is found in folk belief and in many major religions. {{ill|Judaism|ja|ユダヤ教|lt=Judaism|lt_ja=ユダヤ教}} laid down many detailed rules of defilement from early times, which influenced {{ill|Islam|ja|イスラム教|lt=Islam|lt_ja=イスラム教}} in matters such as {{ill|Food taboo|ja|食タブー|lt=food taboos|lt_ja=食タブー}} and still shape the way of life of many people. The defilement concepts of {{ill|Historical Vedic religion|ja|バラモン教|lt=Brahmanism|lt_ja=バラモン教}} passed into modern {{ill|Hinduism|ja|ヒンドゥー教|lt=Hinduism|lt_ja=ヒンドゥー教}} and also influenced {{ill|Buddhism|ja|仏教|lt=Buddhism|lt_ja=仏教}}. Treating {{ill|Menstruation|ja|月経|lt=menstruation|lt_ja=月経}} and women as defiling comes from ancient Indian thought and the Buddhism it influenced.

The opposite of ''kegare'' is purity or holiness, but both defilement and holiness are kept at a distance as {{ill|Taboo|ja|タブー|lt=taboo|lt_ja=タブー}}, and when only the taboo is stressed the two cannot always be told apart. In Judaism, for example, animal blood is as forbidden as food as an {{ill|Unclean animal|ja|不浄な生き物|lt=unclean animal|lt_ja=不浄な生き物}}, but this is because it is holy, "for the blood is the life" ({{ill|Book of Deuteronomy|ja|申命記|lt=Deuteronomy|lt_ja=申命記}}), not because it is defiled.

A related idea in Judaism and Christianity is expressed in the {{ill|Bible|ja|聖書|lt=Bible|lt_ja=聖書}} by the word {{ill|Sin|ja|宗教における罪|lt=sin|lt_ja=罪}}; the sin committed by {{ill|Adam|ja|アダム|lt=Adam|lt_ja=アダム}} is humanity's {{ill|Original sin|ja|原罪|lt=original sin|lt_ja=原罪}}.

== Japan ==
''Kegare'' is an idea of Buddhism and Shinto: a state that falls short of the ideal, such as {{ill|Uncleanliness|ja|不潔|lt=uncleanliness|lt_ja=不潔}} or {{ill|Impurity|ja|不浄|lt=impurity|lt_ja=不浄}}. It is often grouped with ''tsumi'' as ''tsumi-kegare''. People defiled by death, epidemic disease, childbirth, menstruation, {{ill|Crime|ja|犯罪|lt=crime|lt_ja=犯罪}} and the like were barred from taking part in the community: from {{ill|Matsuri|ja|祭事|lt=religious rites|lt_ja=祭事}}, from attending at court, and, for {{ill|Hunting|ja|狩猟者|lt=hunters|lt_ja=狩猟者}} and {{ill|Charcoal burning|ja|炭焼き|lt=charcoal burners|lt_ja=炭焼き}}, from entering the {{ill|Mountain|ja|山|lt=mountains|lt_ja=山}}. Postwar {{ill|Folkloristics|ja|民俗学|lt=folklore studies|lt_ja=民俗学}} has read ''kegare'' as ''ke-gare'', "the withering of ''ke''", the everyday vital force, which is restored by ''hare'' rites such as {{ill|Matsuri|ja|祭|lt=festivals|lt_ja=祭}} (driving out ''kegare'', "making the ''ki'' good", that is, purifying). See also {{ill|Hare and ke|ja|ハレとケ|lt=hare and ke|lt_ja=ハレとケ}}.

=== In Japanese mythology ===
In {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話|lt=Japanese mythology|lt_ja=日本神話}} it appears in the {{ill|Ōharae no Kotoba|ja|大祓詞|lt=Ōharae no Kotoba|lt_ja=大祓詞}} as {{ill|Amatsu-tsumi and kunitsu-tsumi|ja|天つ罪・国つ罪|lt=amatsu-tsumi and kunitsu-tsumi|lt_ja=天つ罪・国つ罪}}. The ''amatsu-tsumi'' are breaking down the ridges between rice fields, filling in the irrigation ditches, removing the sluices, sowing seed over seed, planting stakes, flaying alive, flaying backwards and defecating in sacred places. These were the deeds of Susanoo, who later restored his honour through ''misogi'' and ''harae'' and by killing the {{ill|Yamata no Orochi|ja|八岐大蛇|lt=Yamata no Orochi|lt_ja=八岐大蛇}}.

{{ill|Izanagi|ja|イザナギ|lt=Izanagi|lt_ja=イザナギ}}, returning from {{ill|Yomi|ja|黄泉の国|lt=Yomi|lt_ja=黄泉の国}}, performed ''misogi'' to wash away the defilement of Yomi, and in the course of it many gods were born, including the {{ill|Mihashira-no-Uzunomiko|ja|三貴子|lt=three noble children|lt_ja=三貴子}}; gods were born even from the defilement that was washed away. The first "defilement of death" is the death of the weaving maiden when Susanoo flung a flayed piebald horse into Amaterasu's hall. (The word "defilement" itself first appears in the ''Kojiki'''s story of Yomi. It is never said there that Izanami is defiled; the one defiled is Izanagi.) Izanagi's defilement in the Yomi story consists in breaking a taboo, by following Izanami into Yomi and trying to bring her back.

=== Shinto and Buddhism ===
Both are concerned with defilement, but they differ most in their view of death itself: Shinto treats death and blood as defiling, while Buddhism does not regard death as defiling in the way Shinto does. Funerals may be held at a temple in Buddhism, but in Shinto they are held at home, not at a shrine, which is sacred ground. This reflects a difference in what is held sacred. The purifying salt is used to purify oneself after defilement, and the rosary is wound round the left hand to purify a hand regarded as unclean. Because the state of mind at a death is considered most important, not only the dead person but their relatives are generally not allowed into sacred ground during the {{ill|Mourning|ja|忌中|lt=period of mourning|lt_ja=忌中}}. On the other hand, some shrines enshrine the dead as gods, and {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|lt=kofun|lt_ja=古墳}}, which are tombs, are regarded as sacred ground. In Buddhism, death is part of the cycle of rebirth, the way the world is, and there is no idea that denies it; one seeks instead to escape from that cycle. Buddhist defilement is something to be avoided because it accumulates as latent force ({{ill|Karma|ja|業|lt=karma|lt_ja=業}}), and rests on a reasoned basis.

For the Japanese, {{ill|Kami|ja|神|lt=kami|lt_ja=神}} were supernatural beings, both feared and revered (as in {{ill|Goryō|ja|御霊信仰|lt=goryō belief|lt_ja=御霊信仰}}). The dead were purified, and the souls of particular dead people were enshrined as gods. These gods and defilement cannot coexist, and the {{ill|Temizuya|ja|手水舎|lt=temizuya|lt_ja=手水舎}} at a shrine is there to purify the defilement of the outside world.

Japanese Buddhism is syncretised with Shinto in many places, and the ideas of the two are often mixed (torii at temples, architectural styles and so on). The same is true of defilement.

=== Origin of the idea ===
Many of the forms of Buddhism brought to Japan in the Heian period held this idea, and the idea of defilement spread from {{ill|History of Kyoto|ja|京都の歴史|lt=Kyoto|lt_ja=京都}} throughout Japan. From the late Heian period, more of the high-ranking monks ({{ill|Gakuryo|ja|学侶|lt=gakuryo|lt_ja=学侶}}) who performed rites for the protection of the state and for the emperor and nobles came from the imperial family and nobility. Since they served the emperor, the presiding figure of the rites for the gods, they had to keep themselves pure, so they stopped taking part in funerals and other events likely to bring contact with defilement, which were left to lower-ranking monks called {{ill|Dōshu|ja|堂衆|lt=dōshu|lt_ja=堂衆}} and to reclusive holy men. This was one cause of the growing stratification of the clergy.<ref>Uejima Susumu, "<Ō> no shi to sōsō", in ''Nihon Chūsei Shakai no Keisei to Ōken'', Nagoya University Press, 2010, ISBN 978-4-8158-0635-4 (originally published 2007).</ref> At the same time, Japanese ideas of defilement developed in complicated ways, intertwined with Shinto ideas and with the concept of {{ill|Mourning|ja|服喪|lt=mourning|lt_ja=服喪}} introduced by {{ill|Ritsuryō|ja|律令法|lt=ritsuryō law|lt_ja=律令法}}, and were institutionalised. The ''{{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|lt=Engishiki|lt_ja=延喜式}}'', compiled in the early tenth century, lists "defiling evils" in its third book, on occasional rites, including death, childbirth and eating the meat of the six domestic animals, and mentions defilement elsewhere too.<ref>Harada Nobuo, ''Rekishi no Naka no Kome to Niku: Shokumotsu to Tennō, Sabetsu'', Heibonsha, 1993, ISBN 4-582-84147-3, pp. 102–103.</ref><ref>Yamamoto Kōji, ''Kegare to Ōharae'', expanded ed., Kaihō Shuppansha, 2009, ISBN 978-4-7592-5253-8, p. 16.</ref><ref>Torugawa Masataka, "Heian jidai ni okeru kegare kannen no hen'yō: jingi saishi kara no bunri", ''Nihon Shisōshigaku'' 41, 2009.</ref><ref>''Engishiki'', vol. 1, Nihon Koten Zenshū Kankōkai, p. 106 (National Diet Library).</ref> (The ''Engishiki'''s measures of avoidance were not meant to bar people from taking part, but to set when they should return to duty after a fixed period.) {{ill|Fujiwara no Sanesuke|ja|藤原実資|lt=Fujiwara no Sanesuke|lt_ja=藤原実資}} understood Japanese defilement to be something unknown in India and China (''Shōyūki'', Manju 4.8.25), and {{ill|Fujiwara no Yorinaga|ja|藤原頼長|lt=Fujiwara no Yorinaga|lt_ja=藤原頼長}} pointed out that the rules on defilement are found not in the {{ill|Ritsuryō|ja|律令|lt=ritsuryō codes|lt_ja=律令}} (imported from China) but in the {{ill|Kyaku-shiki|ja|格式|lt=kyaku and shiki|lt_ja=格式}} (enacted in Japan) (''Ukai Zasshō'', Ninpei 2.4.18).

=== Relation to Shinto ===
Research by scholars such as {{ill|Yoshihiko Amino|ja|網野善彦|lt=Amino Yoshihiko|lt_ja=網野善彦}} has shown a close connection between outcast groups and the emperor. One theory sees the emperor as the highest holder of the function of purification. {{ill|Takatori Masao|ja|高取正男|lt=Takatori Masao|lt_ja=高取正男}} held that the idea of ''kegare'' was transformed by the Buddhist notion of impurity.<ref>Takatori Masao, ''Shintō no Seiritsu''.</ref>

As for its relation to ''harae'': ''harae'' originally did not mean removing defilement, but the act by which the person responsible offered goods to the gods as an apology (a property penalty for ''amatsu-tsumi'' and ''kunitsu-tsumi''). Cases have been pointed out at medieval Japanese shrines in which ''harae'' itself was suspended or postponed for a time because of defilement.<ref>Watanabe Shun, "''Kasuga Kiyoharae-ki'' no kisoteki kōsatsu", in ''Chūsei Shakai no Keibatsu to Hō Kannen'', Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2011, ISBN 978-4-642-02899-8 (originally published 2010).</ref>

The {{ill|Haraekotoba|ja|祓詞|lt=haraekotoba|lt_ja=祓詞}} say that the {{ill|Haraedo no Ōkami|ja|祓戸大神|lt=Haraedo no Ōkami|lt_ja=祓戸大神}} purify sins and defilement.

== Death as a source of kegare ==
The ''kegare'' of death still has considerable force in Japanese society,<ref name="scheid">{{cite web|last=Scheid|first=Bernhard |title=Kegare|url=http://www.univie.ac.at/rel_jap/an/Shinto#Kegare|work=Religion in Japan|publisher=University of Vienna|accessdate=2 Nov 2010|language=German}}</ref> even at Buddhist funerals. Death and everything connected with it are seen as a primary source of defilement.<ref name="scheid"/>

This is why, after the death of one of its members, a family will not send friends and relatives the usual seasonal greeting cards in summer and winter, sending letters of apology instead. Those who attend a Buddhist funeral receive a small bag of salt to purify themselves before they return home, so as not to bring ''kegare'' to their families.<ref name="eyfells">{{cite web|last=Eyfells|first=Eyjolfur|title=Shinto's spiritual value in the past and present|url=http://skemman.is/is/stream/get/1946/3342/10458/1/Eyjolfur_Eyfells_fixed.pdf|publisher=Skemman|accessdate=17 October 2012}}</ref>

The family's ''kami'' must be protected as far as possible from contact with death, blood and disease. A still common consequence is that people give up the traditional New Year visit (''{{ill|Hatsumōde|ja|初詣|lt=hatsumōde|lt_ja=初詣}}'') to a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|lt=Shinto shrine|lt_ja=神社}} if there has been a death in the family within the past year.<ref name="scheid"/>

Shinto priests ({{ill|Kannushi|ja|神主|lt=kannushi|lt_ja=神主}}) are expected to take particular care to avoid this kind of ''kegare'' and to deal correctly with death and disease. Given how important dealing with death is in religion, so strong a death taboo cannot have been part of ''kami'' worship from the beginning;<ref name="scheid"/> excluding death from religious rites first became possible when another religion, Buddhism, could take charge of it.

== Notes ==
* In {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|lt=Ryukyuan Shinto|lt_ja=琉球神道}} the defilements of blood and death are disregarded. {{ill|Atsumu Wada|ja|和田萃|lt=Wada Atsumu|lt_ja=和田萃}} suggests that "this may be connected with the fact that the Japanese Shinto that reached Ryukyu at the end of the Middle Ages was {{ill|Kumano faith|ja|熊野信仰|lt=Kumano faith|lt_ja=熊野信仰}}", and that "Ryukyu has a strong faith in the east, but no faith in the west like Japanese Pure Land belief".<ref>Ueda Masaaki and Kamata Jun'ichi, ''Nihon no Kamigami: "Sendai Kuji Hongi" no Fukken'', Gakuseisha, 2003, ISBN 978-4479840633, pp. 77–78.</ref>
